title: Inflation and retirement: why you need to invest
subtitle: Inflation impact on retirement
openingQuestion: Mr. Son sets aside 2 billion VND by holding only cash and a no-term savings deposit for the 20 years before retiring, instead of investing in stocks/bonds. With Vietnam's average inflation of about 3-4%/year, what happens to the real purchasing power of that 2 billion VND after 20 years?
openingOptions: Its purchasing power will rise considerably, since money automatically becomes more valuable the longer it's held, regardless of inflation
Its purchasing power will stay exactly the same, since the nominal figure on the savings book never changes over those 20 years, unrelated to inflation
Its purchasing power falls sharply: 2 billion after 20 years will only be worth about 1 billion
Inflation has no effect on cash whatsoever - it only affects the value of stocks on the stock market
explanation: Inflation quietly erodes the purchasing power of money over time. At an average inflation rate of 3.5%/year, purchasing power falls to about half after 20 years (the rule of 72: 72/3.5 is about 20 years for value to halve). Holding cash or a no-term deposit (very low interest) barely offsets that erosion, leaving Mr. Son retiring with far less real purchasing power than he originally planned for.

diagram.label: A few percent of inflation a year erodes purchasing power
After twenty years, purchasing power is roughly halved
To keep real value, long-term money has to be invested

realWorldExample.description: Vietnam's CPI inflation over the past two decades has swung considerably: some years under 1% (2015), but also periods exceeding 20%/year (2008, nearly 23%; 2011, about 18%). Long-run average inflation is usually estimated around 3-4%/year during recent stable periods, but investors should note that inflation can spike during periods of economic instability, making holding only cash or a no-term deposit far riskier than its outward appearance of 'safety'.

quiz.question: Why is holding only cash or a no-term deposit for many years considered a RISK to a retirement plan, even though the nominal amount doesn't fall?
options: Because the nominal balance gradually falls with each year held
Because a no-term deposit can be frozen indefinitely by the bank without any prior notice
Because inflation erodes purchasing power faster than the no-term rate earns
Because cash is subject to annual personal income tax
quiz.explanation: This is called 'inflation risk' - a quiet but real kind of risk, different from a stock's short-term price swings. Money sitting still at a low interest rate still 'loses value' over time because of inflation.

quiz.question: Why does investing in growth-capable assets (like stocks, real estate) protect purchasing power better than cash over the long run?
options: Because their returns are exempt from personal income tax
Because they never lose value over a long enough horizon
Because they're automatically and precisely repriced every single month according to the CPI index
Because over the long run they typically grow faster than inflation
quiz.explanation: No asset guarantees a return, but historically over long periods, stocks and some other growth assets tend to deliver a positive real return (after subtracting inflation), while cash almost always has a real return near zero or negative.

quiz.question: At 3.5%/year inflation, how long until the purchasing power of money falls to half?
options: About 20 years, using the rule of 72 divided by the inflation rate
About 50 years, since inflation only acts slowly and accumulates very gradually
About 10 years, since inflation compounds exponentially every single year
It can't be determined since inflation varies differently from year to year
quiz.explanation: The rule of 72: 72 divided by 3.5 gives about 20 years. That means 100 million today buys only what 50 million buys today, twenty years from now - and someone retiring at 60 has to live with that for the rest of their life.

quiz.question: Why is putting all your retirement money into a savings deposit risky over the long run?
options: Because the bank could go bankrupt overnight and depositors would lose their entire deposit instantly
Because the after-tax interest rate is often just at or below the inflation rate
Because savings deposits are taxed at a very high personal income tax rate
Because savings interest is only ever paid once, at the deposit's maturity
quiz.explanation: Nominal safety isn't real safety. If a deposit pays 5% while inflation is 4%, your purchasing power only grows 1% a year - and in many periods, that figure has even been negative.

quiz.question: Which asset class has historically kept pace with inflation best over the long run?
options: Long-term fixed-coupon bonds, since interest is paid steadily every year
Cash kept in a safe, since a banknote's face value never changes
Stocks, since a business can raise its selling prices as input costs rise
Gold bars, since the gold price always rises exactly in line with inflation each year
quiz.explanation: A business is a bundle of real assets with pricing power - when overall prices rise, its nominal revenue and profit tend to rise too. That's why stocks are still needed even inside a retirement portfolio.

quiz.question: How should a retiree handle inflation risk?
options: Raise the annual withdrawal rate to 8% to make up for purchasing power lost to inflation
Move everything into a deposit right at retirement to avoid all volatility
Withdraw all the cash and keep it at home to spend freely as prices rise
Keep a portion in stocks so the portfolio keeps growing throughout retirement
quiz.explanation: Retiring at 60 means the portfolio still has to work for another 25-30 years. Moving everything into a non-growing asset trades volatility risk for the risk of running out of money - and the second risk is the one that can't be undone.

keyTakeaways: Inflation quietly erodes the purchasing power of money over time, even when the nominal balance doesn't fall
Vietnam's inflation has had sharply volatile periods (once exceeding 20%/year), making holding only cash/a no-term deposit riskier than its outward 'safety'
Investing in assets capable of long-term growth (stocks, diversified funds) is the main tool for protecting purchasing power against inflation
A retirement plan needs to be calculated in REAL returns (after subtracting inflation), not just the nominal return figure

practicePrompt.question: Mrs. Xuan, 55, has 1.5 billion VND set aside for retirement 15 years away, and keeps it entirely as cash at home because she's 'afraid of losing money by investing'. Based on the impact of inflation, what risk does this approach carry?
options: The biggest risk is that the purchasing power of 1.5 billion gets eroded by inflation over 15 years, while the cash earns nothing
There's no risk at all, since keeping cash at home is the only way to guarantee absolutely never losing money under any circumstances
The only risk is that the cash could be stolen, completely unrelated to inflation or purchasing power
There's no meaningful risk, since inflation in Vietnam is always 0% and doesn't affect the value of cash
practicePrompt.explanation: Holding cash for 15 years lets inflation erode its purchasing power with nothing to offset it - this is a quiet but real risk, even though the nominal figure stays 1.5 billion VND.

application.title: Try the math right now
application.message: Take the retirement savings figure you're targeting and divide it by 2 - that's roughly the real purchasing power after about 20 years if you hold only cash/a no-term deposit at 3.5%/year inflation.
application.secondary: This number is usually more shocking than you'd expect - that's exactly why you need to invest.

sections.text: Many people think the safest way to prepare for retirement is to hold cash or a savings deposit, staying far away from any market risk. But there's a quiet risk that this approach is actually carrying: inflation risk.

Inflation is the phenomenon of goods and services rising in price over time, so the same amount of money buys less in the future. For a retirement plan - which typically accumulates over decades - the impact of inflation is extremely important, because it determines whether the money you save will actually be enough to live on once converted into real purchasing power at retirement.

In recent years, Vietnam's inflation has been relatively stable, usually around 3-4%/year. But looking further back, there have been periods of spiking inflation - such as 2008, when CPI rose nearly 23%, or 2011, when inflation was around 18%. This shows that inflation isn't always low and predictable, and a cautious retirement plan needs to account for the possibility of inflation spiking unexpectedly during some periods.

items: The rule of 72: divide 72 by the inflation rate to estimate the number of years for purchasing power to fall to half (3.5%/year inflation -> about 20 years; 6%/year inflation -> about 12 years)
Cash and no-term deposits have almost no positive real return after subtracting inflation
Term deposits usually pay a higher rate but can still run at or below inflation during some periods
Stocks, diversified funds, and some other growth assets tend to outpace inflation over the long run, despite sharp short-term swings

sections.label: A concrete numerical illustration
sections.text: If you hold 500 million VND as cash/a no-term deposit (near 0% real return after inflation) for 25 years at an average inflation rate of 3.5%/year, that amount's real purchasing power at retirement would be worth only about 215 million VND in today's terms. By contrast, investing in a diversified portfolio earning an average real return (after inflation) of 5%/year, that same 500 million VND could grow to a real value equivalent to more than 1.6 billion VND after 25 years.
Why this is the core reason to invest, not just save

This is the thread running through this entire track on portfolios and retirement: plain saving (keeping money unchanged, not invested) isn't enough to protect purchasing power over decades if inflation exists - and inflation almost always exists in every economy. Investing in assets capable of real growth (after inflation) is the active way to keep your wealth from being quietly eroded over time, which matters especially for a plan with as long an accumulation horizon as retirement.

lines: Inflation is the quiet but certain enemy of every long-term financial plan - it doesn't cause an immediate loss like a market crash, but it erodes purchasing power steadily, year after year.

Investing in assets capable of growing faster than inflation, instead of holding only cash, is the key to making sure the money you save today still means something real when you need it at retirement.
